name: Dusky Blue-Green
lede: Dusky Blue-Green is a dark, grayed teal first plated by Robert Ridgway in 1912, almost indistinguishable on screen from Dusky Bluish Green, its own near-twin.

sections.title: A 1912 plate, with a near-twin
sections.body:
Ridgway's *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* of 1912 plates this swatch at plate XXXIII, hue 39 double-prime, on an aged, scanned original that is itself approximate [1]. The ISCC-NBS charts of 1955 file block 151 as a dark grayish green, 6.7 units from this swatch [1]. The name pairs *dusky* with [[blue-green]] [1].

At hex #455E57 it measures lightness 38 and chroma 11 in LCH, close to gray [1]. Its closest named neighbors are [[dusky-bluish-green|Dusky Bluish Green]], just 2.7 units away and bluer, and [[dusky-green|Dusky Green]], also 2.7 units off and greener; the two Ridgway plates sit near enough to read as the same color on most screens [2]. [[invisible-green|Invisible Green]] sits 3.9 units off, bluer still [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This match appears in 1.59% of the 23,781 paintings in our archive (378 paintings, as photographed); the within-painting lens narrows that to 167 [3]. In our archive it is more common than 68% of the named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 1.9% of the 1,674 paintings we have from that decade (32 paintings), 2.5 times the rate its museums would predict [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 37% of its 167 appearances by lightness rank within the painting [3]. Its most devoted painter is Émile Bernard, present in 4 of 22 works here, 6.4x the baseline of the museums those works come from (as photographed 5.0x) [3]. It is most over-represented in France, 2.2x expected (58 of 3,443 paintings) [3]. The earliest match dates to 1301, 611 years before the name's 1912 record, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin and a look-alike hue in an aged photograph is not proof of a pigment or dye [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so the match is a screen comparison, not a pigment identification [3].
